ego.name: Johann Lukas Schönlein
ego.summary: Johann Lukas Schönlein was a German physician and professor who helped shift German medicine from speculative natural philosophy toward empirically grounded bedside clinical practice. He held major clinical posts in Würzburg, Zürich, and Berlin (Charité), emphasized systematic physical diagnosis and autopsy-clinic correlation, and influenced a large cohort of later leaders in internal medicine and pathology.

category_summaries.summary: The Wikipedia extract provides limited family detail, but it does document Schönlein's son Philipp and his premature death during a research expedition. No named parents or spouse appear in the provided text, restricting the family network to documented relatives.

Schönlein’s academic web runs from early mentors (Röschlaub, Tiedemann, Walther, Döllinger, Oken) to large cohorts of pupils formed by his bedside-centered clinical method in Würzburg, Zurich, and Berlin (e.g., Virchow, Griesinger, Lebert, Traube).

His major posts at Würzburg (Juliusspital), Zurich (new university clinic), and Berlin (Charité) connected him to elite patients and patrons, culminating in service as physician to Friedrich Wilhelm IV.
Friendships and liberal circles mattered most in the Würzburg crisis of 1832 (e.g., Wilhelm Joseph Behr) and in long-running personal ties like Ludwig Rumpf.
